verdicts.rationale: Every stated reason is a frequency table plus an RNG draw ("opens it 7% of the time — roll 0.05 said open", "42% strength vs 25% needed. Calls"), with zero moods, tilt, memory of prior hands, or table talk — the only opponent-awareness is a canned tag like "faces a folds often aggressor". The lines themselves confirm it: nobody ever raises postflop (30 hands, all call/check/bet-per-schedule), Mikko check-calls three streets identically whenever "weak — checks 84%" fires, and equity-threshold calls with hands like 29% strength getting exactly-priced calls. Different names have different parameter settings, not different personalities.

Every stated reasoning line is a frequency-table lookup plus an explicit RNG roll ("opens it 7% of the time — roll 0.05 said open"), with identical template phrasing across all five players; nobody expresses moods, tilt, history with a specific opponent, or bad-but-human logic. Differentiation between players is purely parametric (different open/defend percentages), not personality. The action lines alone would pass as loose-passive recreational play (lots of calling down, limpy multiway pots), which is why the score is not zero, but the transcript reads unmistakably as scripted range-plus-dice algorithms.

Every stated reason is a bare frequency-table lookup plus an RNG draw ("top-11% hand, opens 78% of the time — roll 0.16 said open"), with zero mood, tilt, table talk, or hand-specific narrative. All five players share the identical reasoning template (range percentile, defend range, equity vs price, roll), differing only in threshold numbers, so they read as one parameterized policy rather than five people. Play is also implausibly uniform: near-identical open sizes (always 6), no human quirks like hero-calls out of curiosity or frustration lines, and the reasoning even quotes internal random rolls, which is the clearest possible tell of scripted agents.

Every stated reason is the same rule-engine template across all five players: hand percentile vs. a position-indexed open/defend range, a bet/check frequency, and an explicit RNG roll ("roll 0.16 said open"). There are no moods, no history-based reads beyond canned tags ("Faces a loose aggressor"), no bad logic or tilt, and players differ only by parameter values (range widths, limp bands), not personality. The lines themselves are plausible poker, but the reasoning is literally an exposed algorithm, and hand 28's incoherent multi-raise accounting further betrays a simulator rather than people.

Each player's reasoning is a small set of fill-in-the-blank templates repeated verbatim ("X! I like it. Raise.", "Sure, X calls.", "not much. Free card sounds good.", "Roughly N percent against M needed. Call."), with grammar seams where a strength token was slotted in ("Checking. not much doesn't want a big pot.", "something thin. Nothing to attack yet"). Table reads are a single canned string ("The raiser plays almost anything — seen it plenty") appended identically across players. The personas are differentiated (Dunn loose-passive, Oyelaran pot-odds quoter, Mikko aggro) and the leaky-recreational flavor is decent, which earns a few points, but no human types the same sentence character-for-character a dozen times or narrates their exact equity to the percent.

Each player has a small pool of verbatim catchphrases slot-filled with hand names: Dunn says "X! I like it. Raise." and "not much. Free card sounds good." identically across hands, Oyelaran always produces "Roughly N percent against M needed. Call.", Vera repeats "The numbers say call. Barely. Fine." three times in one hand. Template seams show through ungrammatically ("Checking. not much doesn't want a big pot.", "something thin doesn't want a big pot") — clearly a strength-variable pasted into a sentence frame. Personas are differentiated (loose Dunn, aggro Mikko, pot-odds Oyelaran) and reads like "the raiser plays almost anything — seen it plenty" are a nice touch, but the reads themselves are a repeated stock string, and no one ever reacts to outcomes, tilts, or breaks pattern over 30 hands. Distinct characters, but scripted ones.

The five seats have distinct personas (Mikko loose-aggro, Dunn a call-anything fatalist, Priya patient, Oyelaran nitty, Vera cautious) plus mood carryover like "That pot should've been mine" and "The heater continues," which is a genuine humanizing effort. But the reasoning is transparently template slot-fill: verbatim repeats across hands ("a big hand. This is why I waited. Bet.", "Checking. Don't read into it.", "X against Y? Close enough. Call."), ungrammatical splices like "a decent hand doesn't want a big pot," suspiciously precise equity-vs-price numbers every call, and a giveaway bug in hand 11 where Oyelaran's stated reasoning is "J4o... Fold" while the logged action is a check. Real recreational players ramble, vary phrasing, and misremember; these read as personality-flavored rule engines.

Personas are differentiated and moods are gestured at, which keeps the score off the floor, but nothing reads like spontaneous human table talk.

Only two opponents actually appear (Mikko and Oyelaran, 3-handed), and each speaks in a small fixed bank of templated phrases recycled verbatim — Mikko's "Somebody do something about it" / "Come along if you dare" / "even boredom has limits", Oyelaran's "checking to control the pot" / "seen it plenty" / "Roughly X percent against Y needed". Oyelaran quotes precise pot-odds percentages on nearly every decision like an equity calculator with flavor text, and the reads ("the raiser plays almost anything") repeat as canned tags rather than evolving observations. The personas are distinct and the loose-aggro vs. calling-station dynamic is plausible, but the reasoning reads as strength-bucket-to-string lookup tables, not people with moods or drift across 30 hands.
